#1275. Valverde played over 40 minutes injured as Real Madrid face three away games in a week

Real Madrid came away from Camp Nou on Sunday night with three points and a new fitness worry. José Mourinho revealed after the 2-1 win over Barcelona that Fede Valverde had spent a large part of the game carrying an injury, and the timing is far from ideal with three away fixtures to come in the space of seven days.

The coach went out of his way to single out the Uruguayan in his post-match press conference, saying Valverde “played injured for more than 40 minutes”. Mourinho added: “He got injured, wanted to continue, pushed himself to his limits, and gave everything while he was on the field.”

Mourinho did not say what kind of injury Valverde had suffered or at what point in the match it happened. At the time of writing, Real Madrid had not published a medical report on the midfielder, who was named in the starting XI alongside Aurélien Tchouaméni, Bernardo Silva and Jude Bellingham.

The club’s English account still made him one of the faces of the night, sharing a Valverde post shortly after midnight.

🗣️ @FedeeValverde 🗣️ pic.twitter.com/iOcHUMmM90

Real Madrid C.F. (@realmadriden) October 26, 2026

Valverde was not the only fitness story of the weekend. Thibaut Courtois dropped out on matchday because of what the club called a flu-like illness, with Illia Voloshyn called up as cover. Andriy Lunin started in goal and, according to Real Madrid’s own match report, made a fine stop from a Gerard Martín header in the 66th minute.

Mourinho said his only message to Lunin before kick-off was simple: “You train to play, not to sit on the bench. Go and play.” He also stressed that the squad had not been rattled by the late change, adding that “today none of us cried before the match because Thibaut wasn’t playing”. Courtois, whose future has been discussed in terms of a possible one-year contract extension, now has a few days to recover before the next game.

The calendar offers Madrid little breathing space. Mourinho pointed out that “on Sunday we play away; then we play away on Wednesday, and then we have another away match on Saturday”. According to the fixture list, those games are against Racing Santander on 1 November, AEK Athens in the Champions League on 4 November and Valencia on 7 November.

That run is where Mourinho’s faith in his squad will be tested. He insisted after the Clásico that “I have a rich bench, with players who can be starters”, and he backed it up at Camp Nou by leaving Eduardo Camavinga among the substitutes days after his strong display in the 4-1 win over RB Leipzig. Camavinga came on and set up the late winner for Kylian Mbappé.

The victory was Madrid’s fifth in a row and, as Mourinho noted, leaves them three points behind Barcelona rather than six or nine. Keeping that momentum through three away games will be far easier with Valverde available, so the club’s next medical update on the midfielder will be closely watched before the trip to Santander.

#1274. Footy Fix: Who will win Ballon d'Or as Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe, Lamine Yamal, Lionel Messi vie for prize

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The attention of the soccer world will be fixed on London to start the week, where a months-old question will finally be answered: Who's going to win the Ballon d'Or? I'm Pardeep Cattry with a lookahead to Monday's ceremony, plus a preview of what's to come as action resumes in the EFL Cup.

Monday, Oct. 26🇫🇷 Ligue 1: Paris Saint-Germain vs. Lyon, 3:30 p.m. ➡️ beIN Sports🏆 Ballon d'Or ceremony, 4 p.m. ➡️ DAZN

Tuesday, Oct. 27🇮🇹 Serie A: Roma vs. Cagliari, 3:45 p.m. ➡️ Paramount+🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 EFL Cup: Fleetwood Town vs. Arsenal, 4 p.m. ➡️ Paramount+

Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo may no longer be the frontrunners for the Ballon d'Or, but their decades-long command over soccer's most prestigious individual accolade still colors the way we all look at the award. The air of mystery that should be a fixture in the run-up to an awards show still feels foreign, the ability to gauge the eventual winner a fresh challenge for many. That's especially true this year, particularly on the men's side, where none of the usual indicators apply.

A handful of deserving players make up the list of nominees once again, but none fit the prototype of an eventual Ballon d'Or winner, rightly or wrongly. The award often goes to the best player on a team that won the biggest prize on offer in the last year, a path that would lead you straight to Spain's golden ball winner, Rodri. The midfielder hardly feels like a slam-dunk pick after spending much of last season building his form following an ACL injury, which might lead you to a member of Paris Saint-Germain's UEFA Champions League-winning team. Vitinha, the Portuguese midfielder, might actually have a shot but there are buzzier names in the mix that are equally worthy. The favorite might actually be someone else entirely – Harry Kane, the England captain and Bayern Munich talisman who has steadily established himself as his generation's greatest goalscorer over the years. Here's James Benge on Kane's case in the final batch of Ballon d'Or power rankings.

There is no obvious candidate on the women's side, either, though Alexia Putellas might just be the favorite if the usual patterns apply. The voting body will be inclined to select someone from Barcelona's UEFA Women's Champions League-winning side and with three-time Ballon d'Or winner Aitana Bonmati out of the running after dealing with a broken leg last season, Putellas playing a central role with eight goals and six assists in Europe before leaving for London City Lionesses in the summer. She is one of eight members of that squad among the list of nominees, the list of 30 an eclectic selection of some of the world's best players. The NWSL's nominees include Temwa Chawinga, the league's back-to-back MVP with the Kansas City Current and the headliner for a Malawi side that made a run to the Women's Africa Cup of Nations, and U.S. women's national team standout Rose Lavelle, who scored the game-winner for Gotham FC in last year's NWSL Championship.

#1273. Newcastle jeers tell Matthias Jaissle his ‘vertical’ football is not working

Newcastle United look like a poor team playing badly. The evidence is increasingly damning after Matthias Jaissle’s side were loudly booed off at the end of this limp defeat.

This has all the makings of a long, hard season. Anger is already rising to the surface, even though Jaissle claimed Newcastle deserved more from a game they “controlled” in the first half and “dominated” in the second. Those comments jarred with what we had just seen.

After four years of enjoying an upward trajectory under Eddie Howe, the team faded last season, sold their best players in the summer, lost the manager and there is no evidence yet they have replaced anything with better.

This was supposed to be a reaction to the embarrassing 4-1 thrashing at Coventry City, but it led to another loss and, in the first half at least, another abject display. Aston Villa were always the more fluent and more threatening. They should have won by more than just Johan Manzambi’s first-half header.

Johan Manzambi heads Aston Villa in front! 🟣 https://t.co/jxZf2568Sl

It is getting hard to comprehend what Jaissle wants his team to do. The much-hyped “vertical” style looks like an ugly incarnation of the long ball football of yesteryear. They did not like it at Newcastle in the 1980s and 1990s and some fashions should never return. It is in danger of resembling a shell suit that has emerged from the back of the wardrobe for a Saturday night out.

There is so much confidence in the German in the Newcastle boardroom that they believe improvement is inevitable, but that is far from assured. Newcastle are not getting better; they are making all the same mistakes and, if anything, as an attacking force, they are looking increasingly stale and predictable. They did not have a shot on target in the first half and, other than one fantastic save in the second, Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki had nothing to do.

"If he doesn't slip Harvey Barnes in, he's got to hit the target" Shay Given discusses Newcastle's decision-making in the final third 🔲 https://t.co/wh4kCAEbxV

“Our decision-making in the final third was lacking today,” Jaissle said. “I am frustrated, I understand the supporters’ reaction, that is their right [to boo after a defeat at home].”

It is time for a sharp dose of medicine on Tyneside. Expectations need to be adjusted, especially as none of the new signings have impressed. This was always the fear and the risk when you put all your faith in young players from abroad.

For Jaissle’s vertical football to work, Newcastle need to be able to win the ball high up the pitch, whether that is with a high press or competing for second balls from long passes. They do not do either well. More worryingly, they look so vulnerable, so easy to play through.

Villa did it to them all afternoon. Nicolas Jackson should have scored in the first half, Ibrahim Mbaye should have hit the target in the second.

On another day, Newcastle could also have had centre-back Sven Botman sent off for a lunge on Jackson. Then it really would have become ugly, but the Dutchman survived a VAR check.

Villa were always the better side. There was no fluency in Newcastle’s game, no structure, no patterns of play. Every time they turned over the ball, they looked stretched. Every time they got a set-piece, it was defended easily. Every time they went forward in the first half, the ball was sent aimlessly long and came straight back at them. In the second, they huffed and puffed but did not sustain any pressure on the Villa goal. The missed chances late on were not clear opportunities and they were snatched at by the hapless Yoane Wissa.

Yoane Wissa fails to hit the target after an inspiring run! ❌ https://t.co/ohabzLZBRv

It was largely poor and so was the manner in which Villa took the lead. João Gomes was given the time and space to loft a cross to the far post for Manzambi, who had drifted away from Lewis Miley, to head home.

Newcastle were in disarray and it should have been 2-0 almost immediately when Emiliano Buendía received the ball in the middle of the area and crashed a shot against a post.

The home crowd tried to remain patient and supportive, but the sight of yet another long, aimless ball being punted forward straight to a Villa defender tipped some over the edge. There were boos and jeers in the stands while Jaissle screamed at Joe Willock and Wissa. There were more boos at half-time; things felt combustible.

Newcastle needed a big second half. They were better, but it was hardly anything to get excited about. A shot on the turn from Botman, superbly saved by Suzuki. Then a few half-chances were squandered, the occasional flash of a threat and that was it.

"That was too easy" Matthias Jaissle discusses Aston Villa's winner against Newcastle 🗣️ https://t.co/deg1ALxVBR

#1272. Premier League Power Rankings: Manchester United falling fast; Tottenham Hotspur, Bournemouth rise

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Eight games into a campaign, patterns are supposed to emerge as teams begin to lock into midseason form. This season of the Premier League is no exception, except the pattern is a new one – expect chaos until further notice.

Several teams are experiencing a regression to the mean after rocky starts to the season, evidenced by the weekend's most notable games. Aston Villa are surging up the table after a 2-1 win over Manchester City, Bournemouth defeated Manchester United in style with a 3-0 triumph at Old Trafford and Tottenham Hotspur have gone from zero wins to two in a week, a 2-0 win at Chelsea their most impressive performance in months. Others are also putting their early season results behind them, but it feels like they are crashing back down to earth – Brentford were held to a 1-1 draw at Hull City, while Ipswich Town were unimpressive in a 1-1 draw against Nottingham Forest.

A fascinating theme is beginning to emerge along the way. It feels like there are more midtable teams than usual, even if some sit as high as seventh (someone has to, after all). Then there are those that seem like relegation contenders but are several spots above the drop zone because, somehow, there are that many teams worse than them. There's a frenetic feeling to the Premier League table and, by extension, the latest edition of power rankings but the show must go on.

Here's how each Premier League team is looking after the latest round of games.

Arsenal's 2-0 win over Everton was not glamorous but the Gunners won't care. They're level on points with Manchester City and well-positioned to compete for the title, much as they have been all season.

Manchester City's short-lived grip on first place is gone after their defeat to Aston Villa, one that raises questions about their ability to go the distance in Enzo Maresca's first season in charge.

Liverpool are slowly but steadily figuring things out with Andoni Iraola at the helm, a 2-0 win over Brighton and Hove Albion their most impressive result yet. A top-four spot feels like a realistic aim for this season, even if they are not the finished product just yet.

Fabian Hurzeler's side played a fairly even game with Liverpool, so their stock should not drop too much but the Reds did map out a plan to neutralize their attack-minded tendencies, which might be something opponents borrow from in the coming weeks and months.

This is where the extreme midtable energy of the Premier League comes in – Chelsea were deeply unimpressive against Spurs, unconvincing at almost every turn. Most teams in England's top flight, though, are worse off so the Blues hang onto fifth for now but they will be worth keeping an eye on.

Between a 3-0 win over AC Milan in the UEFA Europa League and their triumph at Old Trafford, it has been a fun week to be a Bournemouth fan. Those wins are a sign that things are finally clicking – they might be 13th in the league but they rank third on expected goal differential, a signal that things were always trending in the right direction.

Aston Villa's slow start is officially a thing of the past, Unai Emery's side smartly outmaneuvering City to prove just that. They are officially a team on the rise.

Leeds United's unstylish but effective consistency means they continue to hang out in the top half of the table but playing even against an unimpressive Sunderland side is not the kind of thing a team earns plaudits for.

There's no reason Brentford should not target a top-half finish but much like Leeds above them, an even game against relegation contenders Hull City is not indicative of the team's overall qualities.

Manchester United really have their hearts set on scaling down the table as fast as they can, don't they? The Red Devils should be better than this but their mistake-prone nature continues to be costly.

A win over Coventry City is one thing but a victory at Chelsea is another. More specifically, it's the kind of thing that ensured Spurs would dig themselves out of their early season hole and perhaps sets them up for some more normal results in the short-term.

There is no shame in losing to the reigning champions but Everton did not make much of a dent in the match, the Toffees seemingly resigned to being permanent residents of the middle of the Premier League's table for the foreseeable future.

For all their faults, Fulham have done well enough to pick up the points expected of them, the latest coming in a win over Coventry City. Barely cracking 0.5 expected goals along the way, though, is not something to write home about.

Conventional wisdom suggests that the other shoe will drop for Hull City but it hasn't yet, especially after picking up a well-earned point against Brentford.

Add Nottingham Forest to the list of anomalies this season, sitting firmly in the relegation zone despite ranking fifth in the league on expected goal differential. Case in point – they tallied 2.29 expected goals to Ipswich's 0.46 but tied 1-1 anyway. Until they solve that problem, they are doomed to less-than-ideal spots on the table.

Ipswich were lucky to pick up a point against Forest but the early season success is a thing of the past for them, too.

Eighth-place Newcastle United seem to be riding their luck – they rank 19th in the league on expected goal differential – but creating a five-point cushion above the drop zone by way of a win over Crystal Palace counts for something.

Sunderland will value the point they picked up against Leeds but they are in the midst of an unexciting season, which is hardly a position of strength for a team in desperate need of points.

Palace will take some solace from the fact that they outplayed Newcastle but in their case, the results actually reflect their form.

Coventry were neck-and-neck with Fulham on expected goals in defeat but considering the Cottagers put up a paltry number, there's not much the newly promoted side can brag about.

#1271. Chinese brands drop Mbappé as backlash hits LaLiga coverage in China

Kylian Mbappé is facing the biggest commercial crisis of his career in China. Three Chinese companies announced on Tuesday that they are ending their agreements with the Real Madrid forward, and the fallout has already reached LaLiga’s television coverage in one of football’s most valuable markets.

The trigger was a short clip linked to the French online show The Bridge. In it, Mbappé is asked which meme of himself he likes most, and he refers to a video of “a guy … I think he was a Chinese dictator”, before an edited picture of his face on the body of Mao Zedong appears, as reported by the Associated Press. The footage has not been independently verified and, according to the BBC, the show has since taken the original upload off its YouTube channel.

Beverage firm Dongpeng, the dairy group Mengniu and Milkground, which makes cheese, all issued statements on Tuesday in very similar language. None of them spelled out exactly what Mbappé had said, but each referred to hurt national feelings. Dongpeng’s statement, carried by the state-run Global Times, ended with the line: “Effective immediately, we are terminating all cooperation with Kylian Mbappé.”

Mengniu said it “firmly opposes and has zero tolerance for any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people”. Social platform RedNote, whose own content partnership with the player ran out at the end of 2024, said it would take down related promotional material. The Global Times added that Dior, On and Hublot had removed Mbappé content from their Weibo pages, and that new users are currently unable to follow his accounts on RedNote or Weibo.

The row has even reached China’s foreign ministry. Asked about the controversy, a spokesperson said that “words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with joint opposition from all sectors of Chinese society”, according to AP.

The part of the story with the widest reach for Spanish football concerns broadcasting. According to the Global Times, Shanghai outlet The Paper reported that China Media Group, the parent organisation of state broadcaster CCTV, has suspended broadcasts of matches involving LaLiga and Mbappé. CCTV’s news apps have also removed content about the striker. Neither LaLiga nor Real Madrid had commented publicly at the time of writing, and there was no indication of how long any suspension might last.

Mbappé himself has not responded either, and The Bridge has stayed silent. The timing is awkward for player and club alike. Only on Sunday he was on the scoresheet as Madrid won the Clásico 2-1 at Camp Nou, a result that came with its own fitness worries over Fede Valverde.

The “dictator” tag has followed Mbappé for some time, partly because of the influence he is said to hold at club and international level, and he has spoken about it before. In a France Football interview in September he said the memes “sometimes reveals a lack of political and human awareness among people”, as quoted by the BBC.

On the pitch, the forward has been in fine form, with goals and assists in recent weeks including the 4-1 Champions League win over RB Leipzig. Off it, the pressure is now on him to address a backlash that is still growing, with Madrid due at Racing Santander on Sunday.

#1270. Who's to blame for Manchester United's decline? Ranking the biggest culprits

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

It's happened again. Another season, another Manchester United crisis. No longer does the end of daylight savings time herald the harsh winter ahead. Instead, it is the boos that ring around Old Trafford as the United faithful turn their ire on the same owners, the same executives and the same players, well aware it will be a different coach that pays the price.

Sunday's 3-0 defeat to AFC Bournemouth was remarkable only for the sheer unremarkability of it. In the 74 years after their first meeting in the 1949 FA Cup third round, Bournemouth won three games against Manchester United. In the last two years they have won three games: all at Old Trafford, all 3-0. Freddie Kruger is treading the boards at the Theatre of Dreams.

Although maybe that analogy is not quite apt. After all, the one positive that you could say about a Krugerian nightmare is that it tends to be a one-and-done situation. No such luck if you happen to be a Manchester United supporter. Could any of them now believe that sacking Michael Carrick would fix anything about this club? They've tried the Eddie Howe-esque Premier League mainstay, the relentless winner a la Antonio Conte, the graduate of the Ralf Rangnick pressing academy in the mold of Julian Nagelsmann. Their shortlist only needs an ex-Ajax coach to sweep the quadrants of post-Sir Alex Ferguson ineptitude. Fred Grim to Manchester United? Well, doesn't that sound about right?

This is a club suffering under profound mismanagement, the sort that no one individual can marshal on their own. So there's plenty of blame to spread around. Let's start doing so, in reverse order of course. Gotta keep you on the page as long as we can. Build some suspense. Who might be top, you wonder? Well you probably know. But you know most every AAA movie is going to end with the hero triumphant. The joy is in the journey to the inevitable end point.

Now look, the soon to be former Manchester United manager is not without his faults, as Bruno Fernandes so robustly articulated after the 4-1 defeat in Como. There have been some very weird technical decisions here this season and a head coach with a scintilla of authority probably could have got this team to stop taking so many shots from outside the box. And yet did anyone at Manchester United genuinely think they'd unearthed the next great coach when they threw him the salvage our season post-Ruben Amorim job?

That Carrick did so much more than that, guiding United to Champions League qualification through a third-placed finish, spoke to his ability to keep things simple. He retained what had worked from his predecessor, tidied up some of the complexities of the formation and rode Bruno Fernandes' player of the season form as far as he could go. It is not his fault that United have not kicked on since. What had the 45 year old achieved in three seasons at Middlesbrough that suggested a coach who would do much more than what most coaches do, get a team to perform at or around its talent level?

Maybe when the stars align, when his team has a game a week and a fully fit squad he could achieve something better than the field but it is no more sensible to project out Carrick's future off the spring hot streak than it is to discount his coaching ability because he has struggled to cope with the first confluence of injuries, unfortunate results and player ill-discipline of his tenure.

Old Trafford seemed to have the right sense of it on Sunday. "It's Carrick you know," reverberated around the ground until the minute he was down the tunnel. Then it was both barrels for everyone else.

No one associated with Manchester United should apologize for having exacting standards. A well-run version of this club would make every decision based on improving their title-winning prospects either in the short or medium term. There should be no need to take the long way to the Premier League summit.

Having said all that, goodness it does not take much to send this club into a doom spiral of nostalgia and despair. When Lisandro Martinez served notice on Jason Wilcox and the hierarchy United had performed pretty well in defeat away to Atletico Madrid, a result that few in the Champions League field could credibly bemoan. Their form had wobbled but only a dodgy Erling Haaland goal had taken Manchester City past them and the last two Premier League results had been disappointing but not disastrous draws.

In short things were not going well but the difficulties were explicable. Up to the loss at the Metropolitano at least one of United's major problems was they had scored fewer goals than their expected goals (xG) for and conceded more than the xG value of their opponents shots. Their actual goal difference was minus-one, their expected goal difference was a shade under plus four. There's some heavy lifting being done in there by thrashing Ipswich Town and Sabah but the aggregate of a good team probably does contain a couple of thrashings as well as games where you play even against seemingly inferior teams like Fulham.

In short, just as United weren't as good as last season's rise to third place -- the defense started wobbling quite dramatically into the spring -- they aren't really as bad as 16th in the table, a point clear of the relegation zone might have you believe. A clear-eyed assessment both of the relative talent of United and the rest of the league would say that this is a good team vulnerable to a wobble. Just stay the course, keep calm in the dressing room and block out the noise.

But, of course... this is Manchester United we're talking about.

Sir Jim Ratcliffe certainly talked a good game when he finally got his hands on the sporting infrastructure at Old Trafford in February 2024, his $1.6 billion investment for around a quarter of the club affording him INEOS Group control of football operations at United. No longer would this be a club in hock to the first team head coach, the Ferguson way of thinking to be replaced by a brain trust that included the sporting director, "probably the recruitment guys" and, for reasons, the chief executive and Ratcliffe himself. "In modern football, you need to decide what's your path and stick to your path," the new minority owner insisted.

In the two and a half years since Manchester United's path has led them to: openly canvass the market for a replacement for manager Erik ten Hag, trigger an extension clause in his contract when they couldn't find anyone better, spend over $400 million outfitting the Dutchman with new players, sack him within four months, hire a coach in Ruben Amorim who had talked himself out of better jobs thanks to his insistence on playing a 3-4-3, finish 15th, sack Amorim just as their analytical profile was on an upswing because he had fallen out with his employers, bring in Carrick temporarily and then permanently, spend almost all their budget on midfielders, get dragged in public by Martinez.

That's just the condensed lowlights. It's fair to say that you don't hear much any more about Project 150, the ambitious vision to mark a century and a half of the club with a 21st top flight title. Perhaps by 2028 sporting director Wilcox will have got round to fixing the defense having blown so much of the 2025 summer budget on attack before then spending nearly $200 million on a midfield that needed upgrades but got Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba while the left back spot was left untouched.

It would say everything about the cataclysmic mismanagement at a senior level if Wilcox -- like so many at the club a man with little top level experience of the role he has been thrust into -- gets the man said to be his preferred choice to succeed Carrick, Eddie Howe.

The same Eddie Howe who spent a hugely successful two years with Dan Ashworth at Newcastle United. The same Dan Ashworth who Manchester United spent £4.1 million on the poaching of and, five months later, firing of. The same Manchester United who in INEOS' period running the show rank ninth in the Premier League for points, 10th for expected goal difference. Still, at least they sacked staff and cut costs. Who ever could have imagined that as a fix for a business' problems?

Speaking after Sunday's 3-0 loss to Bournemouth, Harry Maguire pulled no punches. "At the moment it's nowhere near good enough and something needs to change," he said. He's not wrong. And yet the only constants at this club sit second and first in our rankings. Cast your mind back to the 4-0 thrashing at the hands of Brentford in August 2022, Erik ten Hag's second game in charge and oh, what, half a dozen crises ago. The starting back four for Manchester United on that Saturday evening in west London? Diego Dalot, Harry Maguire, Lisandro Martinez, Luke Shaw. The starting back four in draws against Fulham and Everton more than four years later? Dalot, Maguire, Martinez, Shaw.

There are players at this club who have seen off half a dozen permanent managers. Some might not have lasted that long but in their time they have been frozen out or put up for sale. Few have paid the price for inconsistency. Why would you respect the authority of the head coach if you have spent three or four years in the Old Trafford dressing room and seen so many cycle through without any apparent accountability for the playing staff. It seems notable that Cristiano Ronaldo's bombing out by Ten Hag was followed by one of the most impressive runs of results in the last half decade. Players discovered their actions had consequences and started playing like that.

Now, they talk like they are bulletproof. Imagine Martin Odegaard used a post-match interview to mouth off about Mikel Arteta's tactics. Would he ever play for Arsenal again? That's a question Mesut Ozil and Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang can answer. When a player did not perform for Pep Guardiola's Manchester City, he was swiftly sold. Meanwhile United's squad is preserved in aspic. Their defense moves like it is.

These are not players who lack for talent. United's first choice attack rivals any bar Manchester City and Liverpool. Their midfield needs careful construction to mitigate for its lack of pace but it has quality. When the mood takes them Maguire, Martinez and Shaw are perfectly solid defenders. As the graphic above suggests, this is a team that can have moments of extreme competence. That is how United got to third a few months ago. Were they helped by the coach's tactics or the hierarchy's recruitment? Not really but that does not make these expensive, well-remunerated players innocent bystanders, unable to arrest the decline.

More than two decades after Malcolm Glazer loaded debt onto Manchester United to fund his purchase of the club, what has been accomplished beyond a steady degradation of this behemoth of English culture. Being owned by the Glazers, who have not put any money into the club since the takeover, is estimated to have cost the club at least $1.5 billion, much of it spent on servicing debt from the initial takeover. It should be noted that 15 major trophies have been won in the time the Glazers have owned the club but 10 of them came in the period where Ferguson's sheer magnetism held the club together.

There is an argument to be made that United's commercial income skyrocketed under current ownership and certainly this was a club that was among the first to realize that every region could have its own bespoke set of sponsors, that there was always another billboard or patch on the jersey to splash with a logo. Those brands were not, however, flocking to United because of anything the Glazers had done. United were the dominant force in English football at just the right moment to benefit from the Premier League moving from national to global obsession.

Far from custodians, the Glazers are the most deleterious of landlords. An extractive force, they provide minimal service and value while taking their management fees, dividends, repayments and then the riches Ratcliffe paid for a slice of the pie. All of their money could have gone into retaining United's preeminence in the English game or at least staving off the impact of their indifference. As if to make the metaphor particularly on the nose, on their watch Old Trafford has decayed such that the cost of renovation, an estimated $1.6 billion, might just make a case for the planned new stadium that no supporter seems to want.

A club that even in fallow years ranks among the top 10 revenue generators in football has found itself on a cost-cutting drive for which Ratcliffe is the face both because the Glazers' debt acts as a competitive drag and because ownership showed no interest nor aptitude in improving the on-field product. If the players represent a culture that is accountability-lite then it is ownership that enables it. When we start this piece by warning that nothing will change post-Carrick it is because we have seen enough to know that nothing changes until those who tolerate this degradation of Manchester United are no longer in a position of power.

#1269. 'Players run through brick walls for him': How Scott Parker will fix West Ham - Mark Noble's helping hand, why insiders believe he can shed defensive style... and where it all went wrong for 'distant' Nuno Espirito Santo

Published: 12:00 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 08:44 EDT, 4 November 2026

For a club that prides itself on playing the 'West Ham Way', it has long been impossible to decipher quite what that means these days.

Managers have come and gone with no one able to tell you what their West Ham team embodies. What was the identity under Julen Lopetegui? What was it under Graham Potter? And what, after more than a year in charge, was it under Nuno Espirito Santo? If anything, the longer it went on under Nuno, the more unclear it became.

There had long been concerns in the West Ham dressing room, and boardroom, about Nuno’s confusing tactics, unforgiving man-management and humdrum training sessions. Club insiders described him as distant.

Few can forget the time he played his full backs on the wrong side in a damaging defeat by Brentford and then sent his team out against Leeds with no recognised forward and Andy Irving in midfield.

It was little surprise to see Callum Wilson, the former Hammers striker who started on the bench in those games, liking the club’s Instagram post confirming Nuno had been sacked.

Nor to see current jettisoned midfielder Edson Alvarez do the same when he can’t get into the side despite EFL record signing Arne Engels and Divine Mukasa being overrun every week. And especially not to see the wife of goalkeeper Alphonse Areola, now playing second fiddle to Mads Hermansen, posting an Instagram story to the tune of So Long, Farewell from The Sound of Music.

There had long been concerns in the West Ham dressing room, and boardroom, about Nuno Espirito Santo’s tactics, man-management and training sessions

In Nuno's stead, West Ham have turned to former midfielder Scott Parker to get them out of the Championship

Former West Ham midfielder James Ward-Prowse, another who was bombed out under Nuno, could barely conceal his glee when asked last month after his Southampton side's win at the London Stadium whether it felt even better to get one over a manager who didn’t want you. ‘I’m not gonna lie,' he said, 'of course it does.’

Nuno’s fate is not expected to be mourned for long. West Ham’s supporters had already made their own views clear.

Spurred on by the travelling West Brom fans at the London Stadium on Saturday with their hearty rendition of ’You’re getting sacked in the morning’, the few Hammers left at the end of their 3-1 home defeat joined in.

Three days later, they got their wish. ‘Following a thorough review of the start to the Championship season, the board of directors believe a change is necessary at this time to ensure that the club’s objectives and expectations remain on track,’ read the club statement.

Those expectations are to earn instant automatic promotion, considering West Ham have the most expensive squad in the division and kept hold of Jarrod Bowen after relegation. But they are eighth following those back-to-back defeats by Southampton and West Brom.

It was a surprise to many that Nuno kept his job after relegation. David Sullivan, the former majority shareholder, wanted to sack Nuno in the summer but his influence in the boardroom was fading amid the BBC Panorama expose into historic allegations about his behaviour, which he denies, that saw him stand down as joint-chair.

Daniel Kretinsky, now the man who makes the decisions, wanted to keep the ship steady but has realised a change is needed after their unimpressive start. He made the decision after a crunch meeting this week.

And, so, for their fourth permanent manager since they enjoyed European glory under David Moyes, the Hammers have turned to one of their own former players in Scott Parker, out of work since leaving Burnley in April.

Former West Ham midfielder James Ward-Prowse (centre), who was bombed out under Nuno, could barely conceal his glee after his Southampton side's win at the London Stadium

The club's expectations are to earn instant automatic promotion. But they are eighth following back-to-back defeats by Southampton and West Brom

He will be in charge for the Cardiff game on Wednesday night. They held talks with Parker in the summer and are believed to have done so again last week following the Southampton defeat.

Insiders say the club is acting with more ‘normality’ these days under the leadership of new chief executive Karim Virani, a stark change from the madcap chaos of recent years, and the appointment of Parker, a manager with a track record of getting teams promoted, feels like another step in that direction.

Parker has won three promotions with Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley, with the last coming after racking up 100 points in 2024-25.

And, perhaps even more importantly at a time when the club are still searching for an identity, the 46-year-old – who was named Hammer of the Year three times in a row from 2009 to 2011 – knows what it means to represent West Ham. ‘He knows the West Ham ethos,’ as one senior club source told me this morning.

It’s expected that Hammers legend Mark Noble, currently sporting director and in interim charge, will form part of Parker’s staff. The fans, at least, will have figures in the dugout they can feel connected to.

Parker’s first job will be instilling a resilience that typified his Burnley team. West Ham boast the best attack in the Championship with 33 goals, helped by pumping six past Wrexham and Lincoln, but they have the leakiest defence of any of its top 11 teams.

Eight of their 18 goals conceded have come inside the first 20 minutes and, so far this term, they have failed to win when conceding the first goal.

By contrast, Parker's sides have kept a clean sheet in nearly half of his Championship matches. Burnley kept 30 in their 2024-25 promotion campaign, conceding 16 times in 46 matches and never more than once in a game. West Ham have mustered four clean sheets in their 13 games thus far and have already let in 18.

The 46-year-old - who was named Hammer of the Year three times in a row from 2009 to 2011 - knows what it means to represent West Ham

He will get a helping hand from former team-mate Mark Noble (left), who is now sporting director

Parker is arguably the safest pair of hands West Ham could have placed their promotion hopes in. Those hoping to be freed from the turgid football of Nuno, however, may still be left disappointed.

Parker’s sides do have an identity but it’s one based firmly on being hard to beat. Those who followed Burnley under him say that if they scored even once, they knew they would likely win. ‘Dour but effective,’ was how one Burnley source put it.

Even though they ended the 2024-25 season as the third-highest scorers in the Championship, they ranked only 10th for number of shots and their expected goals (xG). Eight other teams had more touches in the opposition box.

For all the grumbles over his style, Parker’s players loved him. ‘They would run through brick walls for him,’ said one Burnley source. An unusual flurry of long, heartfelt messages from his players followed the decision to part ways.

Those players who had their noses put out of joint by Nuno have a chance to reignite their West Ham careers.

Areola won the player of the season award at Fulham after Parker brought him to the club on loan from Paris Saint-Germain. Noble previously told talkSPORT how much he ‘always respected and liked’ Alvarez as a midfielder.

There’s still a hope among senior figures that having better players at his disposal will allow Parker to play a more attractive style than during his Burnley days. Many who follow the Clarets credit him with being able to build such a resilient team after losing a host of his key players at the end of the transfer window.

The issue, of course, is what happens should Parker get West Ham back up. For all his brilliance at getting teams out of the Championship, his record at keeping them in the Premier League is equally dismal.

Alphonse Areola won the player of the season award at Fulham after Parker brought him to the club on loan from Paris Saint-Germain

Parker was sacked after just four games at Bournemouth in the 2022-23 season

Fulham and Burnley came straight back down, the latter after spending more than £100million in the summer, and he was sacked by Bournemouth just four games in after a 9-0 defeat by Liverpool and complaints his squad was ‘under-equipped’.

Parker has won 55 per cent of his matches as manager in the Championship but only 15 per cent of them in the Premier League. His points per game plummets from 1.95 in the second tier to 0.7 in the top flight.

West Ham and their supporters may well harbour reservations over how they might fare in the Premier League under Parker but, right now, are in no position to think that far ahead. They need to get there first and, more than a quarter of the way through the season, have shown little to suggest they will.

Forget the carnival of free-flowing football for now. After putting up with a circus for so long, a little sense of order might be West Ham’s way back.

#1267. Espanyol sack Manolo González hours after 121st-minute Copa exit at Sestao River

Jon Rojo's goal in the last minute of extra time gave Sestao River a 4-3 win and knocked Espanyol out of the Copa del Rey. Within hours the club ended Manolo González's time as head coach, five months after confirming he would stay with Monchi's full backing.

Espanyol dismissed head coach Manolo González on Tuesday 27 October 2026, hours after a 4-3 defeat at Sestao River in the Copa del Rey. Defender Jon Rojo won the round of 128 tie at Estadio Las Llanas from a G. Zorrilla assist. He forced home a loose ball in the box in the 121st minute, just as the tie looked to be heading for penalties, EFE reported.

The match was played in heavy rain that left the Las Llanas pitch almost unplayable. Marcos Fernández put Espanyol ahead from the penalty spot after six minutes. Adri Carrión equalised in the 18th minute and Andoni Ugarte made it 2-1 in the 40th, both goals set up by Eneko Delgado Ginés.

Espanyol levelled with a second penalty in the 90th minute. Gabriel Moscardo then put them 3-2 up in the 96th minute. Ander Laka equalised two minutes later before Rojo’s late winner.

The visitors had 61% of the ball against 39% for Sestao River. Espanyol completed 321 accurate passes to Sestao’s 140. Sestao still managed 9 shots on goal to Espanyol’s 6, and Espanyol goalkeeper Marko Dmitrović made 5 saves to the hosts’ 2. Ugarte was the top-rated player on the night with 8.5.

Before the tie, the team had taken only one point from their previous 15 available in LaLiga, according to AFP. Their last six results in all competitions now read five defeats and one draw, with losses to Racing Santander, Atlético Madrid, Elche and Rayo Vallecano and a 1-1 draw with Málaga.

Sestao River, coached by Ángel Viadero, have gone the other way. The win over Espanyol extended a run of five wins and a draw in their last six matches.

The club’s announcement brought González’s tenure to a close after more than three seasons in charge. He had reached his 100th official match against Sevilla on 7 September. That made him the ninth-longest-serving coach by matches in Espanyol’s history.

Espanyol finished 11th in LaLiga in 2025/26 under González, with 12 wins, 10 draws and 16 defeats. Monchi, the new sporting director, had given him full backing at that stage.

✍️ OFICIAL | Manolo González deixa de ser entrenador de l'#RCDE. El Club vol agrair-li la seva feina durant tots aquests anys i li desitja molta sort en els seus projectes futurs.

— RCD Espanyol de Barcelona (@RCDEspanyol) October 27, 2026

On the eve of the tie, González admitted results had been poor. He said he would keep fighting for the club until his final day in the job.

Espanyol must now prepare for a LaLiga trip to Villarreal on Friday 30 October. Sestao River travel to Coruxo in Segunda División RFEF Group 1 on Sunday 1 November. The Copa del Rey second round is scheduled for 2 December under the RFEF’s 2026/27 calendar.

#1266. Barcelona headline Women's Champions League Matchday 3 as league phase hits midway point

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 UEFA Women's Champions League will reach the midway point of the league phase as Matchday 3 action kicks off Wednesday. The league phase table hardly looks like a final verdict, with only one team on maximum points, while some clubs are comfortable with split results and others are desperate to keep their campaigns alive. Matchday 3 offers an opportunity to either shake up the table or for clubs to separate themselves, with just four rounds of play left before February's knockout playoffs. Fans can watch all the action across CBS Sports platforms. Paramount+ will livestream matches all season, while select fixtures will also air on CBS Sports Golazo Network and CBS Sports Network. With Matchday 3 split across Wednesday and Thursday, here are four things we're keeping an eye on:

The reigning title holders return to the Champions League with even more hardware than before. The club and several players racked up plenty of honors at the Ballon d'Or ceremony on Monday. The club took home best club, manager Pere Romeu nabbed women's coach of the year, Vicky Lopez won best young talent and Cata Coll was named best goalkeeper.

Alexia Putellas, now with London City Lionesses, was awarded the women's Ballon d'Or, largely for her accomplishments during her final season with FC Barcelona, since the voting period ran from August 2025 to July 2026.

After defeating Paris FC 5-2 on Matchday 1, Barcelona followed up with a 6-0 blowout of Roma on Matchday 2. They're cruising during the league phase, especially with an attack powered by several standouts, including Lopez, Claudia Pina, Kerolin and Ewa Pajor.

Pajor, the Polish international, is now the all-time leading scorer in the Champions League's group and league phases, with 18 goals.

A new UWCL record for Ewa Pajor 👏Her 18th goal makes her the highest scorer in UWCL group/league phase history 👑Stream every UEFA Women’s Champions League game on @paramountplus 📺 pic.twitter.com/2LaFr3y5cj

They'll visit HB Koge on Thursday, and the Danish side is steadily growing into the competition after picking up its first win by beating Servette 5-1. The league phase leaders will be favorites to win, but Koge might not make it comfortable, as they play with nothing-to-lose energy.

OL Lyonnes made one of the biggest statements of the league phase so far with an opening-day 8-0 demolition of Servette, in which Melchie Dumornay scored a brace and Marie-Antoinette Katoto scored a hat trick. They're a Champions League mainstay and perennial contenders, but they were shut out by Chelsea on Matchday 2, with Blues goalkeeper Hannah Hampton putting her stamp on the tournament.

HANNAH HAMPTON STANDING ON HER HEAD 🤯Stream every UEFA Women’s Champions League game on @paramountplus 📺 pic.twitter.com/gd2mxcGJIF

OL Lyonnes will now face another club unbeaten in the league phase, Inter, on Wednesday. Inter have a win and a draw and have shown they are a plucky side to deal with, but if OL want to be lethal contenders, they have to make a statement against the tournament debutants. Dumornay's creativity and Katoto's clinical finishing, with U.S. women's national team defensive midfielder Lily Yohannes anchoring the midfield and a stacked roster around them, will be a tough challenge for any team, especially those newer to the league phase. Chelsea, meanwhile, have to contend with Roma, an Italian squad that's well on its way to another Champions League crashout, showing little improvement in year two of the new league phase format with just one draw over two games. If the Blues could keep OL off the scoreboard, they should be confident they can do the same against Roma, and if they don't, it'll bring more questions about the club's ability to manage Champions League expectations. German side Bayern Munich welcome Real Madrid in a showdown that could tip the league phase table. Bayern had a chance to make an opening-day statement but instead gave up a two-goal lead and settled for a draw against Manchester City, before picking up a crucial win away against Benfica in Portugal. Matches in this competition have often been won or lost late, and veteran Pernille Harder had her say for Bayern at Benfica, scoring her 50th UWCL goal in the 3-0 victory.

50 UWCL GOALS FOR PERNILLE HARDER 🌟She becomes just the fourth player in competition history to reach the milestone 👏Stream every UEFA Women’s Champions League game on @paramountplus 📺 pic.twitter.com/wG9RWk22sl

Real Madrid's two consecutive draws in the competition leave everyone wanting more. Colombia international Linda Caicedo is elite and has consistently shown her quality over the two matches, and if she and Felicia Schroder continue to build chemistry in attack, they'll be a dangerous combo to deal with.

The meeting between the German and Spanish clubs on Wednesday will be a key fixture to watch, as a win for either could put it in a more favorable position in the league phase table at the halfway point.

There were plenty of doubts around Paris Saint-Germain heading into the tournament, given their steep fall from Champions League grace. After a miserable campaign last season, the Parisians got off to another worrisome start with a 1-1 draw against Real Madrid, in which they trailed for over 70 minutes before equalizing from the penalty spot. They quickly followed that up with a five-goal win over OH Leuven on Matchday 2, and now find themselves in a far better position than they were last year. Next up is Manchester City, a side that is still on the hunt for its first win of the tournament. Two sides carefully rebuilding their UWCL pedigree could produce either a cagey matchup or a momentum-shifting performance. Arsenal continue to baffle on the pitch. After a smash-and-grab for all three points on opening day against underdogs HB Koge, the Gunners were challenged by Paris FC in a 2-2 draw the following matchday. Winning ugly doesn't hide the fact that this is a team that has struggled to break opponents down, despite a talented roster, and it raises fair questions about manager Renee Slegers and her tactical approach. Goals from Alessia Russo and Georgia Stanway help, but there is more that's expected from the group that won the UWCL title in 2025, even with Mariona Caldentey managing an injury at the moment. If they struggle against Benfica on Wednesday, it'll cast more doubt on the club's direction this season.

The bottom of the league phase table is already somewhat crowded, even with some unexpected clubs at the moment, but that's what makes the midway point of the tournament so exciting. Manchester City and Real Madrid might steal eyeballs, as neither team can keep drawing for much longer, but former dark horse BK Hacken and last year's dancing debutants OH Leuven have struggled to find the net. Hacken join Servette with zero points through two matchdays and will face Paris FC on Thursday. Paris FC are eager to take the next step in the UWCL, from unpredictable underdogs to bona fide contenders. Whoever drops points in the head-to-head could be out of the race for the top 12 in the league phase.

#1265. Real Madrid striker Kylian Mbappe apologizes after Mao meme comments amid growing backlash in China

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Real Madrid striker Kylian Mbappe issued an apology Tuesday after comments he made about former Chinese leader Mao Zedong led several sponsors to drop him and drew a backlash from Chinese state television. The day after the 2026 Ballon d'Or ceremony, which saw Mbappe leave the London Palladium empty-handed, began with an international drama involving China, Mbappe and LaLiga. It all started when Mbappe told French talk show "The Bridge" that the meme "that makes me laugh the most, it's the one where there's a video of a guy, I think it's a Chinese dictator..." The clip also showed Mbappe's face on an image resembling Mao. To put that into context, a recurring joke, repeated in multiple memes, associates Mbappe with the word "dictator" for his influence in the sport and for how he interacts with teammates and players. During the 2026 World Cup, 2025 Ballon d'Or winner Ousmane Dembele called him "Mbappe Mobut," referring to Mobutu, the dictator who ran the Democratic Republic of Congo for more than 30 years. In September, Mbappe addressed the memes in an interview with France Football, saying that while he understood the jokes, they "sometimes reveal a lack of political and human awareness among people. There's a side that's a bit less funny, because we know the damage people like that have caused throughout history. Being compared to people who murder others, or who have made millions upon millions of people miserable... I don't think I've done that in my life." Two Chinese brands that have deals with the French striker issued statements condemning the player's statements. Mengniu, the country's largest dairy producer, wrote that it, "firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people." Later on Tuesday, drinks giant Dongpeng issued a statement as well. "Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments." According to the state-owned Global Times newspaper, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV's apps won't feature news related to the player, and the broadcaster will also stop streaming LaLiga matches.

Mao is obviously one of the most famous figures in modern China's history. He founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and led the Communist Party until his death in 1976. Much has changed in China since his death, but the Chinese Communist Party still governs the country and sees jokes and memes about Mao as an insult to the party and the nation. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said, "We have noted the relevant reports. Words and deeds that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."

The French striker issued a statement about the matter: "During a recent interview with me, I commented on an image of myself, but my comment was not appropriate, and I now realise that it hurt the feelings of many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world. I apologise to everyone whom my words upset, as that was never my intention at all. I hold deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I express my sincere regret."

LaLiga also issued a statement, defending the agreement they still have in place with Chinese state television. "LALIGA deeply regrets the offence caused to Chinese fans by Kylian Mbappé's recent comments. These comments were made in a personal capacity and do not represent LALIGA. Within the scope of our institutional responsibility, we apologise on behalf of LALIGA and all its clubs. Spanish football stands for respect, coexistence and unity among people from all cultures. We extend our respect to China, its institutions and its people, and deeply value the support of the millions of fans who follow us every week. We reaffirm our commitment to a relationship built over many years. We are working with our partners and institutional counterparts in China to address this situation. Furthermore, in collaboration with clubs and players, we will introduce an awareness and communication protocol aimed at promoting respect for different cultures and helping to prevent similar situations in the future."

LaLiga president Javier Tebas, who recently also had multiple public disagreements with Real Madrid, wrote on X he "cannot allow the actions of an individual to tarnish this relationship or harm the more than 20 clubs competing in our professional leagues and the millions of Chinese fans. We are taking all measures within our power and working directly with our partners and counterparts in China to resolve this situation."

Comunicado Oficial.https://t.co/EfKx1juceJ

Real Madrid have also issued a statement on the topic.

"Real Madrid C. F. wishes to express its apologies to the Chinese people for any discomfort that may have been caused by the recent words of our player Kylian Mbappé. Our club holds deep respect for China, its history, its culture, and its citizens, as well as for the millions of Chinese fans who feel affection and admiration for Real Madrid. The club joins the public apology expressed by Kylian Mbappé, in which the player himself has conveyed his regret for his words and reiterated his respect for the Chinese people. Real Madrid reaffirms its commitment to the values of respect, coexistence, and understanding among cultures, and expresses its desire to continue strengthening the bonds of friendship and affection that unite it with China and its citizens."

#1264. Urda crash: Copa del Rey ties rescheduled to 13 November, three in international break

The RFEF has spread the 24 Copa del Rey first-round ties postponed after the Urda rail crash across 29 October to 13 November. Valencia, Betis and Celta will now play their ties during the November international break.

A national tragedy has stopped Spanish football. The Royal Spanish Football Federation called off every Copa del Rey first-round tie scheduled for the evening of 28 October. All other matches in competitions it organises were postponed too. The decision was taken out of respect for the victims of the rail crash in Toledo province.

A Renfe high-speed train and an Iryo high-speed train collided near Urda station. The crash killed 68 people and injured 80, Público reported. An investigating judge at the court in Orgaz has ordered the first inquiries into what caused the collision.

The shutdown reached beyond the cup. The federation also postponed the nine first-round matches of the futsal Copa de España. The futsal draw planned for 16:00 on 29 October was cancelled.

Valencia, Betis, Alavés, Celta and Levante were the top-flight clubs due in cup action that evening. Each of them must now squeeze a rearranged tie into its schedule. That extra game has to fit into an already crowded run of league and European fixtures. The timing differs sharply from club to club.

Alavés go first. Regional side Anaitasuna host them at 19:00 on Tuesday 3 November. Levante travel to CD Tarancón two days later, on Thursday 5 November.

Three clubs face a longer wait. Celta close the round away to Salamanca, with kick-off at 21:00 on Friday 13 November. Valencia and Betis are in action earlier that same week. A tie that was meant to be settled in October will now be played while national teams are away.

Mallorca’s tie at CD Alcoyano kicks off at 21:00 on the same Thursday evening, after Levante’s game at Tarancón. COPE’s list of the rearranged ties records Mallorca as a Segunda División side, not a top-flight one.

#1263. Are Brighton a Premier League contender? Manchester City EFL Cup match will be biggest test yet

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Is this the year Brighton and Hove Albion make the leap? In their 10th season in the Premier League, the Seagulls have long since moved on from being a side well run enough to keep its distance from the relegation race. Now they might reasonably aspire to another step forward, away from the mass of sides just outside the premium European places and into real contention for Champions League qualification. Indeed, if you are a more exuberant Brighton fan, the question you might be asking yourself is not whether your side has made the leap but whether it has bounded up two tiers over the course of one summer. After all, they sit third in the Premier League table with the division's best attack and its third-best defense; combine those and you have a plus-16 goal difference. Their nearest rival by that metric, Manchester City, is at plus-11. Beat City in the second of this week's doubleheader with Enzo Maresca's side and they will be two points off the league leaders, though Arsenal might well open up a gap. Then again, what do Brighton have to fear from the champions? They've already smashed them 3-0 this season. Even their 2-0 defeat to Liverpool did little to quell Brighton's momentum. Not for the first time in his managerial career, Fabian Hurzeler couldn't resist a snipe at the manager of a big-six opponent in defeat, but he did have a point when he argued that "there was one team who really tried to create and try to win this game." The Seagulls went down swinging at Anfield, drawing seven shot blocks from Andoni Iraola's side. It really was not an exaggeration to say that if Yasin Ayari or Charalampos Kostoulas had scored early on, this might have been another famous win for the boys from the south coast.

Does this all sound too good to be true? Well, then it probably is. Admittedly, Hurzeler's side had looked primed to push on at the end of last season, an impressive run of results in March and April securing an eighth-placed finish and Conference League football. Then, in customary Brighton fashion, their best players left. Danny Welbeck had been their leading scorer, Jan Paul van Hecke the leader in league minutes and a crucial ball progressor, and while Carlos Baleba had endured a down year in which he had battled injuries, he still looked the most likely to ascend to a Moises Caicedo/Alexis Mac Allister level in Brighton's long line of breakout talent in midfield. Brighton could be trusted to replace the players they sold well. Swapping out Van Hecke for Luka Vuskovic already looks like the greatest of swindles on Tottenham, who are happy enough with what they have, even if they might have let the next great center back slip away. It is arguably easier, though, to deal with players you have lost for a fee than with those snared from you by injury. Kaoru Mitoma and Yankuba Minteh were the star wingers in last season's side, the former top 10 in the league for expected possession value added, the latter top 10 for take-ons. These wingers were critical for getting the ball into the box and creating threat when they got there. Injuries mean they have yet to take the field this season. You should not be able to cope with the loss of this much talent for so long. Some of Hurzeler's fixes have been ingenious. Maxim De Cuyper carried plenty of attacking thrust from left back, and after dalliances with a more advanced role last season, he has been converted to it permanently. The careful, steady integration of Kostoulas and Diego Gomez has paid dividends too. Meanwhile, at 35, Pascal Gross is as effective as he has ever been, with four assists and three goals already in this season's Premier League. Gross' pressing has also been critical to Brighton's success. According to data provided to CBS Sports by Gradient, the German international has made eight pressures leading to dangerous situations, placing him in the 99th percentile among Premier League players this season. Kostoulas and De Cuyper are similarly willing runners off the ball, adding up to a team that is even more energetic without the ball this season than it was last. In 2025-26, Brighton led the Premier League in passes per defensive action with 9.3, according to Wyscout. This season they also lead the division in this pressing metric, allowing opponents an average of 7.6 passes per defensive action. It is for that reason that only Wednesday's opponents, Manchester City, allow the other team fewer active minutes in possession than Brighton's 21.5.

Brighton's pressing intensity also means it is not that much of a surprise that they lead the league in counterattacking goals. As they do in goals from corners. As they do in higher-value chances where the shot is worth 0.1 expected goals or higher. As they do too in shots from outside the box. It all looks great, but then the sample size is still only eight games. That might be enough to form the outline of a conclusion in normal circumstances, but Brighton are one of only two teams in the league to have had a man advantage in two games so far this season. It should be said that both Aston Villa and Coventry looked like beaten teams when their player saw red, but we have to take the data set with a pinch of salt when over 10% of it involves Brighton having one more player. (There was also an impressive 33 minutes with 10 men against Sunderland, in which they held on to and ultimately added to a 1-0 lead.) So we should take some of their headline numbers under advisement. Drill deeper and there might be more factors to consider. Brighton lead the league in scoring and are second in xG, but there is a big gap between their 16.2 xG and 23 goals. This is a year in which Brighton's goal-of-the-season contest might be a reasonable proxy for the Premier League's as a whole (Lewis Dunk leads the way for me, Clive). Their shooting form was typified by that 3-0 win over Arsenal. They at least matched the champions in the first half, but they led 2-0 because both Gross and Kostoulas walloped shots in from range. You're not building a title challenge on that. Nor are you necessarily doing the same when you look porous at the other end. It isn't just that Brighton have allowed 11.4 xG to their opponents and are riding a run of shot-stopping that seems unlikely to continue even for a goalkeeper of Bart Verbruggen's quality. Hurzeler's side are also allowing the third-highest xG per shot of any team in the division. Much of that is a function of a worrying set-piece defense, but they are not much better from open play either, allowing 0.117 xG per shot, 10% above the Premier League average. When a team breaks their press like Chelsea did early in the season, that's when they end up in trouble. You don't compete for titles when you are giving up what Brighton are giving up defensively, but then that is a ludicrous conceit in the first place. What is clearly no longer ludicrous is the idea that this team might regularly beat Man City in a one-off match, whether that be the rotated outfit Enzo Maresca is due to field in the EFL Cup on Wednesday or the full-strength outfit that will presumably welcome them back to the Etihad on Saturday afternoon. Indeed, in the reasonably likely event that a sanction obliterates City's standing in this season's Premier League, Brighton could comfortably find themselves among the four or five Champions League qualifiers. The likes of Bournemouth, Nottingham Forest and Brentford are at best performing around Brighton's level so far this season in xG terms but have not picked up anywhere near as many points. Maybe the quality of Liverpool shows down the stretch. Perhaps Xabi Alonso simplifies things at Chelsea. Even then, that probably leaves a fifth spot for an English team to advance to the top tier. There is no question now that Brighton look better placed than anyone else to claim it, propelling themselves into a new class of club. If the experience of the last 10 seasons is anything to go on, this club tends to establish itself quite firmly when it moves up in the world.

#1262. How the US mid-term elections could shake up science

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

The upcoming US mid-term elections could change which political party controls Congress, which meets in the US Capitol building in Washington DC.Credit: Finn Gomez/Getty

As tens of millions of voters head to the polls on 3 November to cast ballots in the US mid-term elections, a political shake-up could be coming to Washington DC — with substantial consequences for the country’s scientific landscape.

Republicans currently hold more seats than do Democrats in both chambers of the US Congress, which has given the party and administration of President Donald Trump unified control of the federal government. But polling data favour Democrats to win back the House of Representatives and suggest that they have a chance of taking control of the Senate, too.

Since Trump took office last year, his administration has terminated thousands of research grants, slashed the federal scientific workforce and sought unprecedented political oversight of science agencies such as the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the US National Science Foundation (NSF). Many researchers and science advocates hope that a new Congress will stand up to the Trump administration to protect science funding and investigate its actions. “The Republican Congress has basically ceded their role in oversight for the last almost two years,” says Shaughnessy Naughton, president of 314 Action, a political fundraising group in Washington DC, which recruits and backs Democratic scientists, engineers and health-care specialists running for office.

The Trump administration has requested deep cuts to federal science budgets for the past couple of years, asking for the NSF’s budget, for example, to be cut by more than 50% in fiscal years 2026 and 2027. Both Republican and Democratic members of Congress, which sets the federal budget, have staved off those cuts so far. But the budget for the 2027 fiscal year, which began on 1 October, has not yet been officially approved.

White House proposes vast overhaul of US science funding: what you need to know

White House proposes vast overhaul of US science funding: what you need to know

Even if Democrats, who have been backing boosts in science spending, were to win control of both chambers of Congress, it could be difficult to push through any major funding increases, because the final budget bills must still be signed by Trump.

At a minimum, researchers and science advocates hope that Congress will continue to prevent big budget cuts. But keeping budgets steady on paper has not stopped the administration from squeezing research in practice. Without congressional approval, the White House has curbed spending in other ways — terminating active grants mid-cycle and refusing to distribute money that Congress had already approved, a controversial tactic known as impoundment.

Science advocates say they hope that a new Congress will assert its budgetary power, namely by pushing back on these actions. The NSF, for instance, closed the 2026 fiscal year on 30 September with some US$1.4 billion in unspent funds, leading to the lowest number of new research grants issued in decades. The agency said that it has two years by law to spend its approved budget.

The Government Accountability Office (GAO), the investigative arm of Congress that has the ability to determine whether funds have been impounded, has rarely pursued action over violations, says Matt Dull, a specialist in government oversight at Virginia Tech, in Blacksburg, but the mid-terms could change the situation.

Controversial White House plan to overhaul US science funding faces Senate opposition

Controversial White House plan to overhaul US science funding faces Senate opposition

Another way that Congress could push back against the Trump administration’s reshaping of US science is to attach specific conditions to funding bills. For instance, because lawmakers haven’t yet agreed on the final budget for the 2027 fiscal year, they passed a ‘stopgap’ bill that funds the government only up to 11 December. The bill contains a section that temporarily blocks a White House plan to overhaul US science.

That plan is controversial: it would, for instance, put political appointees in charge of federal grant review and allow them to override the decisions of scientist peer reviewers. Giving control of grants to political appointees would threaten biomedical progress globally, says Ellie Dehoney, senior vice-president of policy and advocacy at Research!America, a non-profit organization in Arlington, Virginia. The White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB), which created the plan, said it did so to improve transparency, accountability and oversight of federal funds.

Rosa DeLauro, a Democratic representative from Connecticut, issued a statement last month saying that she was confident that Congress would continue blocking the OMB plan in future spending bills.

Although Congress does not run US science agencies, it has oversight powers, which include launching investigations into agency actions. Most of these powers are reserved for the party in control of Congress, and Democrats have pledged to use them if they win big in the mid-terms.

‘Science needs defending’: record number of researchers run for office in US mid-terms

‘Science needs defending’: record number of researchers run for office in US mid-terms

“We will continue the work we have been doing over the past two years to hold the Trump administration accountable,” says Zoe Lofgren, the most senior Democrat on the House Science, Space and Technology (SST) Committee. “If we win, we’ll have more tools at our disposal to do exactly that.” Lofgren and her Democratic colleagues have sent numerous letters to agencies such as the NSF and the US Department of Energy asking about actions such as grant terminations but have received few answers. If Democrats take control, Lofgren, who represents a California district and could become head of the SST committee, would have the ability to issue subpoenas, which can be used to compel administrators to testify in front of Congress.
